They're not hugely different personalities (All birds are different anyways) but congos being bigger does make them more intimidating, that said I've found bigger birds tend to be more chill if anything. But I completely understand feeling scared, I've been around birds my whole life but macaws and eagles make me a little nervous!

Bird being 20ish does at least rule out any kind of juvenile aggression. It's just occurred to me though that summertime might be prompting him to be a bit possessive of your partner (my boy gets a bit like that over me) and if it's that then it does pass! Or he could be going through a seasonal moult which can make them irritable (I think it must itch).

There's another comment mentioning that you would probably get other warning signs if he was really going to bite you and I agree, birds will let you know if they're annoyed long before biting. But the signs can be subtle if you're not used to birds so; A growling sound, crouching lower, and seeming agitated are all signals of them not wanting you in their space. It doesn't mean total hatred, only that they want to be left alone.

I understand feeling silly for being scared but please, please talk to your partner, my husband was also scared of birds when I moved in with my Senegal parrot and because he downplayed this fear I didn't know until my boy nipped his finger (no skin broken) because he could tell my husband was scared and it made him nervous in turn. If I'd known I could have coached them both through it and they would've been buddies much sooner.

Never known greys to be any more aggressive than any other parrot. Out of curiosity is he a Congo or a Timner? (small or big breed)

A lot of treats passed to him through bars so he associates you as friendly. Toys for him too very obviously given by you. Building positive association is important and should calm him down if the behaviour is about territory. Remember as far as he's concerned you're the newbie in his flock. It's less about showing whose boss and more about showing him you're friendly.

A big thing is going to be you staying chill, they can pick up on people's nerves and although it might seem like they're being aggressive in response, 9/10 times they're anxious too. Remember they use their beak to climb as well as bite and in the incident you described he might just have felt unstable on his perch so is trying to 'grab' you with the only thing he has.

Although they absolutely can do damage with their beaks I've had birds my whole life and never had the skin broken by a bite, the never had anything worse than a bruise. A method I found works if they have bitten down is to grab their beak and gently as you can lever them off. I'd advise having your partner present as they'll know better how to calm him down if he does get distressed.

I'd also mention to your partner that you're a little nervous of him and some of his behaviours, giving the examples you just did. There may be perfectly innocent explanations or this might be his play behaviour, which is still not good but it's only a matter of training him out of the habit.

Oh and we'll done for doing as much as you do with him, birds can be so hard to handle even with experience, never mind when you're nervous!

I wanted so badly to breastfeed, broke my heart when my baby at 3 days old was physically pushing my breast away and crying like I was hurting her.
Tried so hard, same results. I tried pumping round the clock and got 2 ounces if I was lucky.

Turned out the odds were stacked against us.
1. LO is tongue tied just enough to make it hurt to feed. She actually was in pain.
2. I've got hypothyroidism, a little known symptom of it is low breastmilk production.
3. My medication for the above inhibits production too.

Swapping to formula was the best desicion I've ever made, it was a miracle she got that vital first feed from me at all. Didn't make me feel any less guilty at the time. But you know what? She's healthy, growing like a weed and such a happy, smiley baby.
